title: Sard's theorem and stratified spaces
summary: Sets of measure zero in manifolds; the measure-zero criterion; Sard's theorem that the critical values of a smooth map form a set of measure zero, with proof; consequences (regular values are dense); stratifications of spaces by manifolds.

objectives.description: State and explain the proof of smooth Sard, including its measure-theoretic and countability hypotheses.
Compute rank strata and distinguish a smooth stratum from its singular closure.
Use dimension and Sard to select a perturbation, and combine this with the compact embedding construction.

preparation.description: Read lectures 10–11: §12 Sard's theorem, Theorem 12.1 (measure-zero criterion) and Theorem 12.3 (Sard) with proof.
Read lecture 12: Definition 13.1 and the examples of stratified spaces.
Read Hitchin appendix §10.5 (Sard's theorem, special case) for the short proof in the equidimensional case.

exitCheck.description: Use the whole problem sheet to sample the listed objectives. Give an independent account of the main theorem and its hypotheses, and solve the transfer/synthesis task. An accepted single exercise is evidence only for its tested capabilities, not whole-unit mastery.

commonMisconceptions.claim: Sard says almost every point in the domain is regular.
commonMisconceptions.correction: It says critical values form a null subset of the target. A constant map can have every domain point critical.

commonMisconceptions.claim: The closed set of matrices of rank at most r is a smooth rank-r manifold.
commonMisconceptions.correction: The fixed-rank stratum is smooth. Its closure includes lower-rank strata and is generally singular.
